evidence: The change started a rollout: a new ReplicaSet (6865675946) was created about 3 s after the change. The new pod's readiness and liveness probes keep failing to connect within 1 s, and these failures are still recurring. The pod was killed and restarted at about 20–26 s. The old pod was then deleted, which left 0 ready replicas at t=30 s. In the last 30 s, 1 of 4 caller requests to emailservice failed, but that is far too few requests to measure an error rate reliably. Server-side latency looks unchanged so far, and checkoutservice is not slower. Because the pod spec changed and the probes fail on a slow start, a resource-limit change is the likeliest cause, most probably a CPU limit set too low. Network-latency changes don't trigger a rollout. One past incident (EXP_0227, emailservice CPU limit set to 125m) had the same events at 30 s and ended High, with repeated restarts and 100% errors. Past incidents with added network latency also ended High. I lowered my confidence because the change itself isn't recorded and there is little traffic. Memory rose slightly (36 to 41 MiB), so a memory limit is less likely but not ruled out. The service is effectively unavailable now, so rolling back is the fastest fix.

The change rolled out a new emailservice pod at t=3s. It failed its readiness probe 4 times and its liveness probe twice while starting up (t=6–17s). After that it passed readiness, because the old pod was removed at t=21s and the rollout finished, with 0 restarts and 1 replica. Caller-side latency is unchanged (p50 3.19→2.94 ms, p95 3.97→3.07 ms) and own-span latency is unchanged (0.27 ms), with 0% errors. But this rests on only 4–6 requests, so the latency evidence is weak. At t=30s the new pod showed CPU 63.8m and memory 72 MiB, against 4m and 36 MiB before. That could be normal startup activity, or the start of pressure from a new resource limit; there is only one sample so far, so I can't tell. Past incidents fit both ways. Rollouts that set a memory limit (64–80Mi) looked like this, with startup probe failures, a completed rollout and no restarts, and ended Low (one ended Medium). Rollouts that set a CPU limit (100–150m) usually already showed restarts by 30s and ended High. No restarts here leans towards Low. No other service is affected. Keep monitoring restarts, memory approaching any limit, and liveness failures over the next few minutes. Roll back if the pod starts restarting or getting OOM-killed.

The change replaced the paymentservice pod through a normal rollout. The new pod was scheduled and started at about 3 s, its readiness probe failed twice in the first few seconds, and the old pod was stopped at 16 s. That sequence fits a change to the pod spec, such as a resource limit. One replica is running with no restarts. CPU jumped to 59m at 30 s, which looks like normal startup work. Memory dipped slightly from 39.6 to 38.1 MiB. In past paymentservice incidents that dip matched memory-limit changes, while CPU-limit changes raised memory by 74-96%. That makes a memory limit the more likely cause, but this is not certain. Paymentservice shows no errors and its median latency is about the same (4.02 ms before, 3.99 ms now). This rests on only 1 request before the change and 4 after, so it is weak evidence. No other service is measurably slower or returning errors. Similar past rollouts mostly ended Low, but some memory- and CPU-limit changes ended Medium or High. Keep watching restarts, OOM kills and checkout latency for the next few minutes.

Callers now see adservice at p50 100.5 ms (baseline 1.47 ms) and 97.9% of its 47 calls in the last 30 s failed. Nearly every call stops at about 100 ms, which looks like the callers' deadline running out. The pod is still running: 1 replica, no restarts, no Kubernetes events, memory flat, CPU low at about 2 millicores, so it is not doing any extra work. A pod that is up but whose callers wait until they time out points to added network delay rather than a crash, CPU limit or memory limit. A past adservice incident with 500 ms of added network latency looked the same at 30 s (latency up over 8000%, 95% errors, frontend slower) and ended High severity with pod restarts. Frontend p50 has gone from 19 ms to 117 ms, but its error rate is still 0%. No other service is measurably slower. Errors above 5% already make this High, so roll the change back now. Confidence is moderate because I can't completely rule out the pod being unreachable for another reason; either way, rollback is the fix.

Callers now see adservice with a p50 of 100.6 ms and p95 of 101.1 ms, up from 1.46 ms, and 96% of calls fail (47 requests in the window). The tight cluster at about 100 ms looks like the frontend's call deadline cutting the calls off, which points to added network delay rather than a crash. That delay is my inference: adservice exports no traces of its own, so I can't confirm it from its side. The pod looks healthy: still 1 replica, no restarts, no events, and CPU (about 2 m) and memory (91.8 MiB) unchanged. Frontend p50 rose from 18.6 to 115.7 ms but it shows no errors, so it seems to give up on ads and carry on. No other service is slower. Past adservice incidents with added network latency (250-1000 ms) all started with the same pattern and ended High, usually with failed health checks, restarts and 0 replicas within about 3 minutes. Errors are already far above 5%, so I recommend rolling back the change.

Callers now see adservice fail on 95% of requests (37 of 39 in the last 30 s, up from 0%). Its p50 latency went from 4.4 ms to about 100 ms, and nearly every call stops at the same ~100 ms point, which looks like the caller giving up on a slow connection. Frontend p50 rose from 21 ms to 116 ms. All other services look the same as before. The adservice pod has not changed: 1 replica, no new restarts, CPU and memory flat, and no Kubernetes events. So adservice is not short of resources and has not crashed, which points to slowness on the network between callers and adservice. Two past adservice changes (400 ms and 500 ms of network latency added) looked exactly like this at 30 s: 95% errors and a slower frontend. Both were High severity, and by 170 s the replicas had dropped to 0, the pod had restarted 3 times and errors had reached 100%. Severity is already High (over 5% errors and more than double the baseline latency), so the change should be rolled back now.

At t=-0.2s the emailservice deployment was scaled from 1 replica to 0 (ScalingReplicaSet event, pod killed). Metrics now show replicas=0 and memory falling from 35 to 2.4 MiB. In the last 30s, its server spans recorded no requests. The one call checkoutservice made to it failed after 0.45ms, an error rate of 100%, though that is only one request. Checkoutservice itself did not fail on that one order (0 errors, 25.6ms against a 28.6ms baseline p50), so the email failure seems not to be passed on to it, but traffic is too low to be sure. With 0 replicas the service is unavailable, which counts as High severity. Recommend rolling back the change to restore the replica.

Callers of paymentservice now wait about 500 ms at p50, up from 2.4 ms, but paymentservice's own server spans are unchanged (0.21 ms vs 0.31 ms). That pattern means roughly 500 ms of added network delay, not slow processing. CPU (about 1 millicore) and memory (about 47 MiB) stayed flat until the restart, so a resource limit is not the cause. Liveness probes started failing about 2 s after the change because they could not connect within 1 s. Kubernetes killed the container at about 22 s, and at 30 s the pod was down: replicas 0, memory 2.3 MiB, image re-pulled. This will likely become a restart loop, which is High severity. Checkoutservice has slowed to match, from 25 ms to 521 ms p50, but frontend has not significantly slowed and no service is returning errors yet. The latency results rest on very few requests (3 recent vs 9 baseline, p=0.0045), though the probe failures and the pod kill back them up. Recommend rolling back the change.

Right at the change, the paymentservice deployment was scaled from 1 replica to 0: the events show the ReplicaSet scaled down and the pod killed. Metrics show 0 replicas at +15 s and +30 s. In the last 30 s, the only call to paymentservice failed (100% errors, 0.41 ms, consistent with the connection being refused) and the service recorded none of its own requests. The one checkout in that window also failed, and frontend errors rose from 0% to 1.2% (85 requests). Payment and checkout traffic is very low (1–3 requests per window), so the error rates rest on a single request. Still, 0 replicas counts as High regardless. Every checkout will fail until the change is rolled back. Other services show no change.

The change rolled out a new productcatalogservice pod (new ReplicaSet created at about 5 s). That pod failed its readiness probe once at 9 s ('failed to connect within 1s'), and the old pod was killed at the same moment. Over the last 30 s, callers saw 21% errors. In the last 10 s, callers saw 100% errors (15 requests, p95 about 11.8 s, so calls are timing out), and the service logged no request spans of its own. The pod is not handling traffic even though replicas=1 and restarts=0. Requests that did succeed in the 30 s window were not slower, which argues against added network latency. Memory dropped to 5.8 MiB, which could fit a memory limit, but there is no restart to confirm it, so the cause is unclear. Knock-on effects: frontend errors at 48% with p95 about 12.6 s; recommendationservice's callers see 24% errors and p95 about 16 s; checkoutservice's 2 recent requests both failed after about 15–19 s (only 2 requests, so weak evidence). A past memory-limit change to this service settled back to Low, but that one never reached 100% errors with no server spans. Past changes that left the service unreachable all ended High. Roll back now.

The change caused a normal rolling replacement of the productcatalogservice pod. At 6.4 s a new pod was created and started. Its readiness probe failed once at 8.4 s and has not failed again. The old pod was killed at 9.4 s. Replicas are still 1, there have been no restarts, and no further warning events. Over the last 30 s the service's own server spans are unchanged (p50 0.09 ms vs 0.1 ms baseline, 0% errors), so there is no sign of CPU throttling or slow processing. On the new pod, memory fell from about 9 MiB to 2.9 MiB and is now 5.8 MiB, and CPU dropped a little, which is consistent with a restart after a resource-limit change. The bad news is all on the caller side, during the handover: 9.4% errors and p95 around 17 s over 30 s, and in the last 20 s all 10 caller requests failed after 17–19 s. That window has no server spans, so these calls never reached the new pod. They are probably connections still held to the deleted old pod. Frontend shows 34% errors in the same window. Past incidents with the same rollout event pattern (EXP_0250, memory limit 64Mi; EXP_0404, CPU limit 100m) had 24% and 5% errors at 30 s. In both, errors were gone and p50 was back to baseline (within 1–2%) by 170 s. Those outcomes were Low and Medium. Network-latency incidents look different: there replicas went to 0 and pods restarted repeatedly. Confidence is limited for three reasons. Requests in the latest window are very few (1 in the last 10 s, and it failed fast). I can't yet see the new pod serving traffic. I can't fully rule out a CPU limit. Watch for the next minute: if caller errors don't clear or the readiness probe fails again, roll back the change.

Events show a normal rolling update about 3 s after the change: a new frontend pod was created and the old one deleted at 15 s. That looks like a pod-spec or resource-limit change, not a network fault. Restarts are 0 and replicas stay at 1. Error rate is 0%. Frontend median latency hasn't moved (17.2 ms vs 17.2 ms baseline, not significant). The slowest 5% of requests (p95) jumped from 27 ms to 109 ms over the last 30 s, and to 263 ms over the last 15 s on 39 requests (p=0.049, so not significant). Two readings fit. One is cold-start noise from the new pod. The other is CPU throttling: the tail gets slower while the median holds, which is what a tight CPU limit does. Past frontend incidents with a CPU limit of 100m followed this same pattern of a rollout with a small median rise and ended Medium; a 64Mi memory limit and a 150m CPU limit both ended Low. CPU usage is about 21 millicores and memory dropped to 5 MiB after the new pod started. No downstream service is significantly slower. Nothing currently meets the Medium bar (median latency or errors), so Medium rests mainly on the tail and past incidents, and confidence is low. Next: in a few minutes, re-check frontend p95 and whether it is being CPU-throttled. If the tail stays high, raise the CPU limit or roll back.

The change has already pushed shippingservice into High severity. Over the last 30 s, callers saw errors on 41% of requests (baseline 0%) and p95 latency of about 19.6 s (baseline 2.3 ms). In the last 10 s, half of the requests failed and median latency was about 2.1 s, against roughly 1 ms at baseline. That 10 s window held only 4 requests, so treat those exact figures with caution. The change rolled out a new pod, and its readiness probe failed within seconds because it couldn't connect within 1 s. There are no container restarts, it still has 1 replica, and CPU is flat. Memory fell from 6.7 to about 3 MiB, which fits a freshly started pod. The damage is spreading: frontend's error rate went from 0% to 17% and its p95 from 32 ms to about 19 s, while all other services look unchanged. Checkout, payment and email served too few requests to compare. The cause looks most like added network latency: the timeouts, the failed connect probe and the stable resources match past shippingservice incidents where latency was injected, all of which ended High, often with 100% errors. A service outage can't be ruled out, since the change itself isn't known. Rolling back the change is the right move either way.

About 3 s after the change, Kubernetes started rolling out a new adservice pod (new ReplicaSet 5dbb89c7d7: Scheduled, Pulled, Started). That means the pod spec changed, most likely a CPU or memory limit, but the telemetry doesn't show which. Nothing is hurting yet. Callers see adservice p50 at 1.23 ms against a 1.29 ms baseline (41 requests in the last 30 s), with 0% errors, 0 restarts, 1 replica and no Unhealthy events. In the last sample (+30 s), CPU jumped from 2m to 96m and memory from 94 to 154 MiB. That fits a Java pod starting up, and I can't yet tell whether the old pod or the new one is serving traffic. No other service is significantly slower (currencyservice +13% p50 but below the significance bar). Past rollouts of adservice limit changes at normal traffic mostly ended Low: CPU 250m Low, memory 200Mi Low, memory 180Mi Medium (+26% latency), CPU 200m Medium. One CPU 200m case at high traffic ended High with latency +269%, and Medium/High could still happen here. Keep watching adservice latency, restarts and Unhealthy probe events over the next few minutes, and roll back if latency rises more than about 20% or the pod starts restarting.

The change replaced the adservice pod. A new ReplicaSet, adservice-6dbbc49859, was scaled from 0 to 1 at t+3s and its container started at t+4s. This usually means the pod spec changed, most likely a CPU or memory limit. There are no restarts, no Unhealthy or Killing events, and replicas stay at 1. Callers see no slowdown: p50 went from 3.88 ms to 3.26 ms (-16%), p95 from 6.77 to 5.33 ms, with 0% errors over 45 requests (not significant). At t+30s CPU jumped from about 13 to 96 millicores and memory from 84 to 130 MiB. That fits a Java service starting up in its new pod. Past adservice incidents that looked the same at 30 s under normal traffic (CPU limit 250m: CPU +566%, memory +77%, p50 -15%; memory limit 180Mi) ended Low. One similar case under high traffic (CPU limit 200m) became High as latency rose by about 270%. Traffic is normal now, so I lean towards Low. I can't see the new limit itself, so confidence is moderate. Keep watching adservice latency, CPU and restarts for the next few minutes, and roll back if latency starts rising or the pod starts restarting.

The change started a rolling update. The new pod (ReplicaSet 7dbdf95d7) failed 3 readiness probes and 2 liveness probes, each one a 1 s connect timeout, and the old pod was killed at t+15s. Since then recommendationservice is failing completely: callers saw 100% errors in the last 10 s (22 requests) and 33% over the last 30 s, and the failures return almost instantly (p50 0.04 ms), which suggests no healthy endpoint. The service's own spans show 0 requests in the last 10 s. CPU jumped from about 12m to 46m and memory stayed flat at about 32 MiB, so memory is not the problem. A pod that cannot answer probes within 1 s on startup fits a restrictive CPU limit (like past incidents EXP_0297 and EXP_0408, both High). Added network latency could look similar, so the cause is not certain. Repeated liveness failures will probably cause restarts or a crash loop. Frontend shows no errors and is not slower, so it seems to handle missing recommendations gracefully. No other service is significantly slower. Roll back the change.

At 30 s nothing is degraded yet. The change started a rolling update: a new ReplicaSet (adservice-98d766b7) was scaled up and its pod was scheduled and started at t≈3-4 s. There are no restarts, probe failures or kills so far, and replicas are still 1. Pod CPU went from about 2m to 88.6m and memory from 93 to 159 MiB. That jump fits a new pod starting up, but nothing yet shows a limit change or what it is set to. As callers see it, adservice is not slower: p50 is 1.29 ms against a 1.27 ms baseline (p=0.27), with 0% errors over 39 requests. Past adservice rollouts with this same 30 s pattern were CPU or memory limit changes, and they ended Low, Medium or occasionally High. Their outcomes only diverged after the old pod was replaced (around 170 s). Telemetry can't yet tell which limit changed, so the cause is unclear. The most likely outcome is little or no impact. Watch whether memory heads toward a limit (OOM kills or restarts), whether CPU latency climbs once the new pod takes all traffic, and whether probes fail during the cutover.

Right at the change, the cartservice deployment was scaled from 1 replica to 0. Events show the pod being killed and the ReplicaSet scaling down, and metrics now report 0 replicas. In the last 30 s, all 31 calls to cartservice failed (100% errors), with p95 latency around 19 s from timeouts. The failures are spreading upstream: frontend errors rose to 91% (p95 about 19 s), and both recent checkoutservice requests failed, though 2 requests is too few to rely on. Other services show only small latency changes that are not statistically significant. Nothing suggests the replicas will come back on their own, so roll back the change to restore at least 1 replica.

Checkoutservice handled only one request after the change, so this rests on very little data. That request took 1244 ms as seen by its caller and 1143 ms in checkoutservice's own spans, against a baseline p50 of about 19.6 ms. That is roughly 60 times slower, far past the 2x threshold for High. The calls checkoutservice made looked slow too: paymentservice took 104 ms as checkoutservice saw it, versus 3.5 ms at baseline, and emailservice took 108 ms versus 2.7 ms. Yet those two services' own spans took under 1 ms. So the delay is in the network on checkoutservice's side. About 100 ms is added to every outbound call, and with many downstream calls per order this adds up to more than 1 s. CPU (about 1 millicore) and memory (8 MiB) are unchanged. There are no restarts and no Kubernetes events, and no requests are failing. Every other service, including frontend, is not measurably slower overall, though frontend's checkout requests inherit the delay. The likely cause is network latency injected into checkoutservice; rolling back the change should fix it.

The frontend's own p50 latency went from 15.75 ms to 5117 ms (p95 6628 ms), with no errors so far. Every call the frontend makes to another service now takes about 500 ms longer: currencyservice 1.5 to 502 ms, productcatalogservice 0.6 to 501 ms, recommendationservice 3.8 to 504 ms, and one checkoutservice call took 518 ms. The receiving services' own request times are unchanged, so the delay is on the frontend's network path, not in those services. A fixed delay like this points to added network latency rather than a CPU limit. Frontend CPU fell from about 19.5 to 12.6 millicores, and memory rose only slightly, from about 14 to 17.5 MiB. Kubernetes health checks on the frontend have been timing out since 8 s after the change, and at 28 s the container was killed and restarted. Those failures are still recurring, so a restart loop is likely. That puts the frontend at High severity: latency is hundreds of times its baseline and it is restarting. Recommend rolling back the change.

Frontend's median latency went from 15 ms to about 10,100 ms (p95 about 13,500 ms). Throughput dropped from 156 to 13 requests per 30 s. Every outgoing call the frontend makes now takes about 1000 ms more. Calls to currencyservice, productcatalogservice and recommendationservice each take about 1001–1004 ms where they used to take 0.6–4 ms. The called services' own spans are unchanged (sub-ms to about 2 ms), so they are processing normally: the frontend's network is adding about 1 s per call, and those calls stack up on each page request. The frontend's liveness probe timed out 5 s after the change, and at t=30 s the pod restarted (restarts went from 4 to 5) and replicas fell to 0. CPU (about 12–18 millicores) and memory (12–15 MiB) are flat and low, so this doesn't look like a resource limit. Downstream services aren't degraded in their own processing. Their traffic has fallen only because the frontend is barely serving. Expect the frontend to keep failing its probe and restarting, so roll back the change.

Callers now wait much longer for productcatalogservice: p50 went from 0.6 ms to 200.8 ms and p95 from 1.77 ms to 202 ms, across 308 requests. Its own server spans barely changed (0.09 ms to 0.11 ms), so the service itself isn't slow. A fixed delay of about 200 ms added between callers and the service points to the network. CPU (~9m) and memory (~11 MiB) are flat, it still has 1 replica, there are no restarts or Kubernetes events, and no errors. The delay is spreading to callers: recommendationservice p50 went from 2 ms to 202 ms and frontend p50 from 16 ms to 1417 ms (frontend calls productcatalogservice many times per page). The one checkout request took 1029 ms, but that is a single request. Latency is already far more than double baseline, so severity is High. Roll back the change.

Measured from the callers' side, checkoutservice p50 latency went from 39 ms to about 8,055 ms and p95 to about 17.9 s, and 6 of 7 calls failed (86% errors). This is well past the High threshold. The one request in checkoutservice's own server spans still took a normal 28 ms. Callers waiting far longer while the server's own work stays fast points to the network rather than slow processing. The new pod rolled out once and its readiness probe timed out once while starting. It shows 0 restarts, 1 replica, and CPU near zero. Memory fell from 8.2 to 3.6 MiB at the last sample, which I can't explain, but with no restarts it doesn't look like a memory crash. Frontend errors rose to 8.1% (significant) and its p95 jumped to 6.2 s, so the impact is reaching users. All other downstream services are unchanged. Past checkoutservice changes that added network latency all ended High. Caveat: very few checkout requests (3 at baseline, 7 since), so the test is not formally significant (p=0.033). The timeouts could also mean the service is partly unavailable, which is why confidence is only moderate.

Only one checkout request has arrived since the change, so this rests on a single sample. That request took 723 ms as the frontend saw it and 673 ms in checkout's own span. Before the change the median was about 24 ms, so this is roughly 30 times slower. Checkout's calls to emailservice and paymentservice took about 52 ms each, against about 2.5 ms before. Those services' own request spans are unchanged (under 1 ms), so the extra time is spent on the network leaving checkout, not inside the services it calls. Checkout's CPU (about 1.5 millicores) and memory (8.2 MiB) are flat, with 1 replica, no restarts and no Kubernetes events, which rules out CPU limits, memory limits and pod failures. No other service is measurably slower, and the frontend's own p50 is unchanged. This matches past incidents where 25 to 100 ms of network latency was added to checkoutservice; all of them ended at High severity. Confidence is reduced because of the single request.

The change rolled out a new currencyservice pod at t≈3.6s. Its readiness probe failed 4 times and its liveness probe failed twice, all with 1s connect timeouts. That points to a slow, CPU-starved startup. The new pod did become ready, because the old pod was removed at 27.6s. It has not restarted, replicas = 1, and there are no errors. CPU on the new pod is about 4x baseline (57m vs 13m) and memory is up about 70% (85Mi vs 50Mi), the usual post-rollout startup jump. Latency as callers see it is almost unchanged (p50 +3–5%, not significant). The server-side p50 is up about 14% over the last 10s, which is a small upward trend. Downstream services, including frontend, are not significantly slower. This matches past incidents where the CPU limit was set to 100m or 140m: the same events and the same CPU/memory jump at 30s, ending in High and Medium. A memory limit is less likely because there were no restarts or OOM kills, and added network latency is ruled out because there was no big jump in latency. Only 30s of data and near-baseline latency so far, so confidence is low. Watch latency and probe failures closely, and raise the CPU limit or roll back if p50 goes above about 20% over baseline or restarts appear.

The change rolled out a new ReplicaSet (emailservice-7555b567d8). Its pod started, then failed its readiness and liveness probes with 1 s connect timeouts. The kubelet killed it and the restart count went from 7 to 8, so the pod is now in a restart loop. CPU went from about 3m to 48m and memory from 36 to 56 MiB, but there was no OOMKilled event. That points to a slow startup from CPU throttling rather than a memory limit. This pattern matches past incident EXP_0354 (emailservice CPU limit set to 100m: new ReplicaSet, probe failures, Killing, CPU up about 900%, ended High). The past network-latency incidents look different: replicas 0, memory down about 93%, and no new ReplicaSet. Latency data is too thin to judge: 1 request in the last 30 s against 10 in the baseline. No other service has been shown to be degraded. A restarting pod already counts as High severity, so I recommend rolling back the change.

The change started a rolling update. A new pod (5d7457449b) was created at t+4s. Its liveness probe timed out twice (t+10s and t+15s) and its readiness probe timed out three times, each failing to connect within 1s. It did become ready, and the old pod was deleted at t+22s. Over that window CPU rose from about 23m to 71m and memory from 34 to 70 MiB, with no restarts yet. No other service is affected yet. Probe timeouts during startup with healthy latency match past recommendationservice incidents where the CPU limit was cut to 100-150m (EXP_0297, 0214, 0215, 0408). The content of the change is not known, so this cause is inferred from that pattern, which lowers my confidence. Recommend rolling back now rather than waiting for the restarts.

Callers saw checkoutservice's p50 latency go from 20 ms to 445 ms, about 22 times its baseline (p=0.008). Its own server spans show the same jump, from 20 ms to 409 ms. There are no errors, no restarts and no Kubernetes events. CPU stays at about 1.5 millicores and memory at about 8 MiB, so a CPU or memory limit is unlikely. The calls checkoutservice makes to paymentservice and emailservice now take about 38 ms instead of about 3 ms, but those two services' own spans are unchanged at about 0.3 ms. That points to roughly 35 ms of delay added to each network call checkoutservice makes. It makes many calls per order (cart, product catalog, currency, shipping, payment, email), which adds up to the roughly 400 ms extra. No other service is slower in its own spans, and frontend's p50 is unchanged, with only its p95 rising, from 33 ms to 82 ms. Latency is far above double the baseline, so severity is High. Confidence is lower because checkoutservice served only 3 requests in the recent window (7 in the baseline).

Frontend's own server spans went from p50 17.6 ms / p95 34.6 ms to p50 405 ms / p95 660 ms (about 23x slower, p=1e-23). Errors stayed at 0%. Every call frontend makes to another service now takes about 35 ms longer (client-side p50 for currency 1.6→36.8 ms, productcatalog 0.8→36 ms, recommendation 4.3→39.5 ms). Those services' own server-side times are unchanged, so the added time is spent on the network around frontend, not inside the other services. Frontend's CPU (about 20m) and memory (about 15 MiB) are flat, there are no restarts and no Kubernetes events, so this is not a resource limit. Latency is far more than double the baseline, so I rate it High and recommend rolling the change back. Checkout, cart, payment, email and shipping got no requests in the last 30 s, so their effect can't be measured yet.

Callers now wait much longer for productcatalogservice: p50 went from 0.66 ms to 76 ms and p95 from 1.9 ms to 77 ms (395 requests, p≈5e-162). Its own server spans barely changed (0.09 ms to 0.11 ms), so the delay is in the network path, not in processing. That steady added ~75 ms looks like injected network delay. CPU (about 10m) and memory (about 10–11 MiB) are flat, with no restarts and no Kubernetes events, so CPU or memory limits are unlikely. There are no errors. Checkout also looks slower (18 ms to 129 ms), but that is based on only 2 requests. Latency is far more than double the baseline, so severity is High. Rolling back the change is recommended.

Checkout calls to paymentservice now take about 152 ms at p50, up from 1.8 ms, which is roughly 85 times slower. paymentservice's own server spans barely moved (0.26 to 0.43 ms), so the extra time is spent on the network, not in processing. CPU (about 1 millicore) and memory (49 MiB) are flat, there is 1 replica with 0 restarts, no Kubernetes events and no errors. The delay passes straight through to checkoutservice, whose p50 rose from 20 ms to 168 ms. Every other service is unchanged. Confidence is limited because paymentservice only served 3 requests in the baseline and 4 in the last 30 s, too few for a reliable statistical test. Still, all 4 slow requests were consistently around 150 ms, well over double the baseline.

The change rolled out a new currencyservice pod (ReplicaSet 6dfcd9c668, scaled 0→1 at t+3s). Since it started, the pod has failed its readiness probe 4 times and its liveness probe 2 times, each a 1s connect timeout on port 7000. That pattern means the process is too slow to answer, which is what heavy CPU throttling looks like. Its CPU went from about 30m to 69m and memory from 52 to 76 MiB at t+30s, and there are no restarts yet. One more liveness failure is likely to get the container killed and restarted. Right now, as callers see it, p50 latency is only 10% higher (1.58→1.74 ms) with 0% errors over 390 requests, and p95 rose from 4.0 to 6.1 ms. Checkout and payment each show 1 error in 7 requests, too few to read anything into; no other service is significantly slower. The closest past incident, a CPU limit set to 100m on currencyservice (EXP_0225), showed the same probe failures and a pod kill and ended High. A tight memory limit is the other possibility: that past case (EXP_0162) had already restarted 5 times by 30s and ended Low. I expect probe-driven restarts, so I predict High and recommend rolling back. Confidence is moderate because nothing has restarted yet and current latency is barely changed.

The change rolled out a new paymentservice pod. The old ReplicaSet was scaled down at about 16 s and the new pod has 1 replica running with 0 restarts. It failed its readiness probe twice in the first 2 s after starting (t≈6-7 s), which is normal while a pod is still booting. CPU jumped to about 55m at t=30 s and memory stayed near 38 MiB, which looks like startup work rather than the service running into a limit. Latency seen by callers went from a median of 2.95 ms to 4.0 ms (+36%), but that is based on only 3 requests and is not statistically significant (p=0.09). Errors are at 0%. No other service is measurably slower; checkoutservice looks up 38% but also on only 3 requests and not significant. Past paymentservice incidents with the same pattern (new pod rolled out after a CPU or memory limit change, CPU spike at 30 s, latency flat) all ended Low. The High-severity past incidents showed 0 replicas, restarts or 100% errors, and none of that is happening here. Confidence is limited because so few payment requests were served and it is only 30 s after the change, so keep monitoring.

The change rolled out a new productcatalogservice pod. Its readiness probe failed with 'failed to connect within 1s: context deadline exceeded' and the old pod was then killed. Callers see productcatalogservice errors at 4.5% (from 0%) and p95 at 10.3 ms (from 2.0 ms). The service's own server spans are unchanged (p50 0.09 ms), and it logged only 73 server spans against 222 caller requests, so the delay and failures are on the path to the service, not in its processing. In the last 10 s only 1 caller request was recorded despite high traffic; it waited about 11 s and failed, and the service logged no server spans at all. Frontend errors are at 20%, its p95 is about 17.6 s, and its last-10 s request also took 11 s and failed. Recommendationservice (p50 +75%) and checkoutservice (p50 +91%, only 3 requests) are slower. This matches past cases where network latency was added to productcatalogservice: probe failures and kills, then 0 replicas and 100% errors within a few minutes, ending at High severity. Confidence is moderate because the last-10 s window has very few requests and one past case (a memory limit) started similarly but recovered.

At t=0.6s the shippingservice deployment was scaled from 1 replica to 0. The pod was killed and replicas have stayed at 0 since. Callers now see 85% errors on shippingservice (baseline 0%), with p50 latency of about 6.3s and p95 about 19.6s (baseline 0.9ms / 2ms). The problem is spreading upstream: frontend errors rose from 0% to 22% and its p95 went from 43ms to 17s. Checkout errors are at 75%, but that is only 4 requests, so that figure is weak. Other services show no change. With no replicas, nothing will recover on its own, so roll back the change to restore the replica.

In the 30 s since the change, callers saw 94.8% of adservice requests fail (baseline 0%), and p50 latency went from 1.2 ms to 100.5 ms. That is about the same as the callers' ~100 ms timeout, so requests are hanging until they give up rather than being answered slowly. Since t+5 s the liveness and readiness probes keep failing because they cannot connect to port 9555 within 1 s. CPU stays low (~4 millicores), memory is flat at 95.6 MiB, there is still 1 replica and no restarts have happened yet. This points to the service not accepting connections, not to a CPU or memory limit. Failed liveness probes will probably lead to restarts, which keeps it High. The frontend has no errors, but its p50 latency went from 16.5 ms to 114.5 ms because it waits out the adservice timeout. Rolling back the change is the fix.

30 s after the change, callers waited about 500 ms for emailservice, up from 2.4 ms (p50). Its own server spans stayed under 1 ms (0.27 to 0.35 ms), so the extra time is on the network, not in processing. The sample is small (6 caller requests, p=0.13), but the evidence lines up. 2 of the 6 requests (33%) failed. I did not check frontend directly. Two past emailservice incidents looked the same (400–450 ms added network latency): the pod kept failing probes and restarting, replicas stayed at 0, errors reached 100%, and both ended High. Roll back the change.

As callers see it, emailservice latency went from about 2.6 ms to about 202 ms, roughly an extra 200 ms per call. Its own server spans barely moved (0.26 to 0.33 ms), so the delay is on the network, not in processing. Emailservice latency is now far more than double its baseline, which counts as High, so I recommend rolling back.
